'''Alexander Weinstein''' (21 January 1897 – 6 November 1979) was a mathematician who worked on [[boundary value problem]]s in [[fluid dynamics]].

== Early life, family and personal life ==
Weinstein was born to Judel Lejb Weinstein and Praskovya Levkovich, his family was [[Jews|Jewish]], and his father was a [[Doctor of Medicine|doctor]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Siegmund-Schultze |first=Reinhard |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1515/9781400831401 |title=Mathematicians Fleeing from Nazi Germany |date=2009-12-31 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-1-4008-3140-1 |location=Princeton|doi=10.1515/9781400831401 }}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Alexander Weinstein - Biography |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Weinstein/ |access-date=2022-06-30 |website=Maths History |language=en}}</ref> His family moved to [[Astrakhan]], but later decided to emigrate to [[Germany]], there Weinstein completed his schooling, having studied first in [[Würzburg]], then at the [[University of Göttingen]] during 1913/14.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Diaz |first=J.B. |date=1973-01-01 |title=Dedication to Alexander Weinstein |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/00036817308839065 |journal=Applicable Analysis |volume=3 |issue=3 |pages=205–208 |doi=10.1080/00036817308839065 |issn=0003-6811|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

After his graduation, he left for [[Zürich]] and soon undertook research for [[Hermann Weyl]] and [[Rudolf Fueter]] and was awarded a [[doctorate]] in 1921 for his thesis on the [[tensor calculus]] and linear groups of matrices.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=Alexander Weinstein's Accademia dei Lincei obituary |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Extras/Fichera_Weinstein/ |access-date=2022-06-30 |website=Maths History |language=en}}</ref> [[Weyl]] suggested Weinstein to several prominent mathematicians, including [[Paul Sophus Epstein]], who was then worked at the [[California Institute of Technology]].<ref name=":0" /> In the end, Weinstein worked as an assistant of [[Leon Lichtenstein]] at the [[University of Leipzig]] in 1922.<ref name=":0" /> In 1924, Weinstein returned to [[Zürich]] and continued his research into [[hydrodynamics]], he published two works on the matter.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Weinstein |first=Alexander |date=1924-12-01 |title=Ein hydrodynamischer Unitätssatz |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01181077 |journal=Mathematische Zeitschrift |language=de |volume=19 |issue=1 |pages=265–275 |doi=10.1007/BF01181077 |issn=1432-1823|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Weinstein |first=Alexander |date=1924-12-01 |title=Der Kontinuitätsbeweis des Abbildungssatzes für Polygone |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01187452 |journal=Mathematische Zeitschrift |language=de |volume=21 |issue=1 |pages=72–84 |doi=10.1007/BF01187452 |issn=1432-1823|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite book |last=Hager |first=Willi |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1201/b11699 |title=Hydraulicians in Europe 1800-2000 |date=2014-03-21 |publisher=CRC Press |doi=10.1201/b11699 |isbn=978-0-429-08802-5}}</ref>

Weinstein was a target of [[xenophobia]], so he struggled to find a "scientific position adequate to his abilities in Switzerland", as such [[Weyl]] recommended Weinstein for a [[Rockefeller fellowship|Rockfeller Fellowship]], with him being awarded it, and spent two years (1926/27) in [[Rome]], where he worked with [[Tullio Levi-Civita|Tulio Levi-Civita]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" /> With [[Tullio Levi-Civita|Levi-Civita]], Weinstein published three more works before he returned to [[Zürich]] as a [[Privatdozent|privatdocent]] in [[Weyl]]'s chair, then in 1928 he was appointed to the [[Hamburg University of Technology|Hamburg Technical University]], he also joined the [[German Mathematical Society]].<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4" /> He married Marianne Olga Louise Ganz on 13 March 1928 in [[Hamburg]], they did not have any children.<ref name=":1" />

By 1933, he was sought by [[Albert Einstein]] as a collaborator in [[Berlin]], however after the electoral success of the [[Nazi Party]], Weinstein, being of [[Jews|Jewish]] background, instead went to [[University of Paris|Sorbonne]] and the [[Collège de France]] in [[Paris]], where he worked with [[Jacques Hadamard]].<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" /> He was awarded the degree of Docteur ès Sciences Mathématiques in 1937, and spent a few semesters in [[England]], at the [[University of Cambridge]], and the [[University of London]], before returning to [[Paris]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":3" /> In May 1940, after the [[Nazi invasion of France]], Weinstein and his wife fled to [[Portugal]] with the hope they could seek [[Refugee|refuge]] to the [[United States]].<ref name=":0" />

They arrived in [[New York City|New York]] on 26 October 1940, and lived at 22 West 75th Street, for the next eight years Weinstein taught at a number of different places, and [[Naturalization|became a citizen]] in 1946.<ref name=":0" /> Together with Monroe Martin, an expert on [[Mathematical analysis|classical analysis]] and [[fluid dynamics]], he founded the Institute of Fluid Dynamics and Applied Mathematics (later renamed the [[University of Maryland, College Park|Institute of Physical Science and Technology]]) at [[Maryland]] in 1949.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":3" /><ref name=":2" />

Weinstein's research covered numerous topics, he is famous for having solved [[Helmholtz resonance|Helmholtz's problem for jets]], giving the first [[Existence theorem|uniqueness and existence theorem]] for free jets in his papers from 1923 to 1929, and he examined many [[Boundary problem (spatial analysis)|boundary problems]], whilst giving hydrodynamic and electromagnetic applications.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":3" /> Weinstein's method was later developed to give accurate bounds of [[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors|eigenvalues]] of plates and membranes, and he introduced a new branch of [[potential theory]] through his examination of singular [[partial differential equation]]s.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":3" />

Weinstein retired in 1967, yet continued research at the [[American University]] in [[Washington, D.C.|Washington D.C.]], he worked from 1968 to 1972 at [[Georgetown University]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" /> In 1972, Weinstein published alongside [https://www.mathgenealogy.org/id.php?id=156429 William Stenger], the book ''Methods of Intermediate problems for eigenvalues'', and then in 1978, when Weinstein was eighty years old, Joe D Diaz made a collection of Weinstein's writings.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":1" /> He died on 6 November 1979, following a [[Surgery|surgical operation]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" />
